guide.title: Golden Gate Park, San Francisco: the Music Concourse, the gardens, Stow Lake and the windmills
guide.intro: Golden Gate Park is a rectangle of about 1,017 acres, half a mile wide and three and a half miles long, running from Stanyan Street to the Great Highway, with the Panhandle carrying on east between Oak Street and Fell Street to Baker Street. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 15 October 2004, reference number 04001137. William Hammond Hall surveyed the site in 1870 and became its first superintendent in 1871; John McLaren held the post from 1890 until his death in 1943, and a man-made forest of over 30,000 trees covers the ground they planted. The Music Concourse holds the de Young Museum, the California Academy of Sciences and the Japanese Tea Garden. West of it are Stow Lake, the Polo Field, the bison paddock, two windmills and the Beach Chalet at 1000 Great Highway.

sections.heading: The Music Concourse, the museums and the gardens
sections.body:
The Music Concourse is the sunken oval at the Stanyan Street end of the park, with the de Young Museum on its north side at 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive and the California Academy of Sciences on its south at 55 Music Concourse Drive. The bowl sits approximately ten feet below the surrounding roadway; its surface is asphalt paths with fields of decomposed granite at the southwest end and turf at the northeast end, planted with a bosque of pollarded deciduous trees, primarily London Plane and Scotch Elm. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 249, designated in 2005 under Ordinance File No. 051590, and the ordinance draws the landmark boundary to include the three pedestrian tunnels that run under the concourse. The Spreckels Temple of Music closes its west end: a masonry and concrete bandshell clad on the exterior with Colusa sandstone, built in 1900 with funds donated by the sugar magnate Claus Spreckels to a design by the Reid Brothers, with a central half-dome and two flanking colonnades of eight pairs of Ionic columns.

Monuments stand around the oval. The Miguel de Cervantes Memorial by Joseph Jacinto Mora, bronze and natural stone of 1916, shows Cervantes looking down at Don Quixote and Sancho Panza kneeling before him. Two cast concrete sphinxes by Arthur Putnam of 1903 flank the footpath entrance to the de Young parking area. The Robert Emmet Memorial by Jerome Connor, bronze on granite of 1919, was the gift of James D. Phelan, and Eamon De Valera, President of the Irish Republic in 1919, spoke at its dedication. The Goethe and Schiller Monument by Ernst Rietschel dates from 1901, the Ludwig van Beethoven Monument from 1915, the gift of the Beethoven Maennerchor of New York and dedicated on 15 August 1915. The Giuseppe Verdi Monument by Orazio Grossoni, a 52-ton statue, was the gift of the Italian Colony of San Francisco.

The Japanese Tea Garden is at 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, open every day from 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. in winter and 9 a.m. to 5:45 p.m. in summer, with the gate closing at 4:30 p.m. and 5:30 p.m. George Turner Marsh created it as a Japanese Village feature of the 1894 Mid Winter Exposition and Makoto Hagiwara designed and constructed it; it was expanded from one acre to five in 1902. The Conservatory of Flowers stands above Conservatory Valley on John F. Kennedy Drive: San Francisco Landmark No. 50, designated in 1972, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, reference number 71000184. It was acquired for the park from an estate while it was still in crates and constructed in 1878.

East of the concourse are the Children's Quarter, the Sharon Building of 1888, which is San Francisco Landmark No. 124, designated in 1981, and the carousel in its 1889 building of sixteen fluted, tapered wood Doric columns. The Shakespeare Garden of 1928 carries six bronze panels with 88 floral quotations. McLaren Lodge, San Francisco Landmark No. 175, designated in 1984, stands at 501 Stanyan Street. Kezar Stadium is at 670 Kezar Drive, and Kezar Pavilion, a gymnasium building of 1926 with seats for four thousand, fronts on Stanyan Street.

sections.heading: West through the park: lakes, meadows and the windmills
sections.body:
Stow Lake wraps around Strawberry Hill in the middle of the park: 12.7 acres, completed along with Huntington Falls in 1893, crossed by the Roman Bridge on the north side and the Rustic Stone Bridge over the south arm, both of 1893 by the architect Arthur Page Brown. Huntington Falls drops approximately 90 feet down the flank of the hill in concrete sculpted to look like natural rock, and the Chinese Pavilion of 1981, a gift from the sister city Taipei, stands at the water. The boathouse at the north part of the lake rents American-made row and pedal boats by the hour and runs a cafe. The San Francisco Botanical Garden is at 1199 9th Avenue: 55 developed acres of a 70-acre site, showing more than 8,000 different kinds of plants.

West of Crossover Drive the park opens out. The Polo Field, formally the Golden Gate Park Stadium, is a 17-acre field inside a 10-foot graded berm with a trotting track on top, with eighteen sections of concrete stands lining the embankment on the north side and another six on the south. Anglers' Lodge of 1936 overlooks fly casting pools 450 feet wide by 185 feet long. Spreckels Lake, approximately six acres, is used for model boating, and the model yacht clubhouse of 1938 stands beside it. The bison paddock is a large fenced open space with a feeding shelter and isolation pens at its west end; bison were introduced into the park in 1890 and the herd was moved to this ground around 1900. The Chain of Lakes, North, Middle and South, were made in 1898.

At the Great Highway end stand two windmills. The Dutch Windmill of 1902 is 75 feet tall on a 5-foot-thick concrete foundation 33 feet across, and is San Francisco Landmark No. 147, designated in 1981. The Murphy Windmill of 1905 is 95 feet tall with a span of 114 feet, and together with the Millwright's House it is San Francisco Landmark No. 210, designated in 2000. The Queen Wilhelmina Tulip Garden lies beside the Dutch Windmill. The Beach Chalet at 1000 Great Highway is San Francisco Landmark No. 179, designated in 1985, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 22 July 1981, reference number 81000172; Lucien Labaudt's fresco People and Places of San Francisco of 1936 is inside it, with a visitor center on the ground floor and a brewery and restaurant above. The Roald Amundsen Monument of red Norwegian granite and bronze stands north of the building.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Steer by the gates and by the addresses.

The gates: Arguello Gate at Fulton Street and Arguello Boulevard, two large pylons and flanking walls of stone ornamented with polychrome terra cotta and copper metal urns and globes; Brown Gate at 8th Avenue and Fulton Street, with a bronze Bear on the northeast corner and a bronze Lion on the northwest corner; Breon Gate at 19th Avenue and Lincoln Way, two large ornamented stone pylons; and two boulder groupings inscribed with the name Golden Gate Park, one at the Great Highway and John F. Kennedy Drive entry and one at the Fulton Street and Martin Luther King Jr. Drive entry.

The addresses: the de Young Museum, 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive; the California Academy of Sciences, 55 Music Concourse Drive; the Japanese Tea Garden, 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive; the San Francisco Botanical Garden, 1199 9th Avenue; McLaren Lodge, 501 Stanyan Street; Kezar Stadium, 670 Kezar Drive; and the Beach Chalet, 1000 Great Highway. The San Francisco Model Yacht Club gives its own location as the 36th Avenue and Fulton Street entrance.

The park runs between Fulton Street on the north and Lincoln Way on the south, from Stanyan Street west to the Great Highway, and the Panhandle carries on east between Oak Street and Fell Street as far as Baker Street. A stone masonry wall of rustic stone-like rectangular blocks runs along Stanyan Street from Fell Street and along Fulton Street to 2nd Avenue.

faq.question: When are the Japanese Tea Garden and the California Academy of Sciences open?
faq.answer: The Japanese Tea Garden at 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive is open every day, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. in winter and 9 a.m. to 5:45 p.m. in summer, with the gate closing at 4:30 p.m. in winter and 5:30 p.m. in summer. The California Academy of Sciences at 55 Music Concourse Drive is open Monday to Saturday from 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and holds Thursday NightLife from 6 to 10 p.m. for visitors of 21 and over. No source states opening hours for the de Young Museum, the Conservatory of Flowers or the San Francisco Botanical Garden, so none are given here.

faq.question: Which buildings in the park carry a register citation?
faq.answer: The Conservatory of Flowers is San Francisco Landmark No. 50, designated in 1972, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, reference number 71000184. The Sharon Building is San Francisco Landmark No. 124, designated in 1981. The Dutch Windmill, recorded as the North Windmill, is San Francisco Landmark No. 147, designated in 1981. McLaren Lodge is San Francisco Landmark No. 175, designated in 1984. The Beach Chalet is San Francisco Landmark No. 179, designated in 1985, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 22 July 1981, reference number 81000172. The Lawn Bowling Clubhouse and Greens is San Francisco Landmark No. 181, designated in 1986. The Murphy Windmill and Millwright's Cottage is San Francisco Landmark No. 210, designated in 2000. The Music Concourse is San Francisco Landmark No. 249, designated in 2005. The park itself was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 15 October 2004, reference number 04001137.

faq.question: What is there at Stow Lake?
faq.answer: A lake of 12.7 acres around Strawberry Hill, completed in 1893 and built with a 10-inch layer of clay under a 3-inch layer of crushed rock rolled into it. Two bridges of 1893 by the architect Arthur Page Brown cross it: the Roman Bridge, a gentle arch of iron-reinforced smooth-finished concrete, on the north side, and the Rustic Stone Bridge, a more steeply arching pedestrian bridge covered with bulging rustic stones, over the south arm. Huntington Falls, approximately 90 feet high, was completed with the lake in 1893, collapsed after a broken irrigation line undermined its foundations in 1962, and was completely reconstructed in 1984. The boathouse at the north part of the lake rents American-made row and pedal boats by the hour and runs a cafe serving from lattes to local wine and from hamburgers to salads; no source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

faq.question: Where are the windmills, and what is the Beach Chalet?
faq.answer: The Dutch Windmill stands at the northwest corner of the park near the Great Highway: built in 1902 to pump water from wells to the reservoir on Strawberry Hill, designed by Alpheus Bull, Jr., 75 feet tall with a 5-foot-thick concrete foundation 33 feet in diameter, San Francisco Landmark No. 147, designated in 1981. The Murphy Windmill stands at the southwest corner: built in 1905 with funds donated by Samuel Murphy, 95 feet tall with a span of 114 feet, and with the Millwright's House it is San Francisco Landmark No. 210, designated in 2000. The Beach Chalet at 1000 Great Highway is a stucco Spanish-Moorish revival pavilion of 1925 designed by Willis Polk, with a visitor center on the ground floor and a brewery and restaurant above, open Monday to Friday 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 179, designated in 1985, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 22 July 1981, reference number 81000172.

faq.question: What is the Panhandle?
faq.answer: A strip one block wide and eight blocks long, running east from the end of the park between Oak Street and Fell Street, from Stanyan Street to Baker Street. It was laid out about 1872, was originally called The Avenue, and was constructed as a connecting carriage road from the edge of the developed city to the park, with a meandering roadway down the centre lined with trees and shrubs to mitigate the prevailing westerly winds. Two paths run its length today, the northern one for bicyclists and the southern one for pedestrians. The William McKinley Monument by Robert Ingersoll Aitken, bronze and marble on granite of 1904, stands at Fell Street and Baker Street, with a fifteen-foot bronze figure representing Justice at the top of its pedestal. A playground and a basketball court stand on the strip; the playground equipment was installed in 1996.

photos.title: The Conservatory of Flowers above Conservatory Valley
photos.description: The wood and glass Conservatory of Flowers of 1878 seen from the south across the planted beds and lawn of Conservatory Valley in Golden Gate Park.
photos.author: WolfmanSF

places.name: Golden Gate Park
places.summary: The park runs between Fulton Street on the north and Lincoln Way on the south, from Stanyan Street west to the Great Highway, with the Panhandle carrying on east between Oak Street and Fell Street to Baker Street. The National Register nomination gives the property as 1,017 acres and describes the park as roughly a rectangle, half a mile wide and three and a half miles long. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 15 October 2004, reference number 04001137.
places.history: William Hammond Hall surveyed the site in 1870 and was appointed the park's first superintendent in 1871, serving from 1871 to 1876 and again from 1886 to 1889; William Bond Prichard held the post from 1876 to 1881, and F. P. Hennessey and John J. McEwen from 1881 to 1882. John McLaren became superintendent in 1890 and served until his death in 1943. In 1871 Frederick Law Olmsted wrote to Hall that the conditions were so peculiar and the difficulties so great that he regarded the problem as unique, and that it must be solved, if at all, by wholly new means and methods, requiring invention rather than adaptation. A man-made forest of over 30,000 trees covers the park, primarily Monterey Pine, Monterey Cypress and eucalyptus; in the eastern part some of the bedrock hills are covered with oak woodlands. Structures put up and later taken away include the First Superintendent's Lodge of 1874, the Casino restaurant of 1881, removed in 1896, the Aviary of 1890, the Suspension Bridge of 1891, and the Richmond-Sunset Sewage Treatment Plant of 1937, removed in 1996.

places.name: The Panhandle
places.summary: A strip one block wide and eight blocks long, running east from the end of the park between Oak Street and Fell Street, from Stanyan Street to Baker Street. Two paths run its length, the northern one for bicyclists and the southern one for pedestrians. A playground and a basketball court stand on the strip; the playground equipment was installed in 1996.
places.history: Laid out about 1872 and originally called The Avenue, the strip was constructed as a connecting carriage road from the edge of the developed city to the park, with a meandering roadway down the centre lined with trees and shrubs to mitigate the prevailing westerly winds. William Hammond Hall's stated intention was to plan and plant this Avenue reservation as a park, to impart a wooded effect, and by the overlapping of suitable tree masses to arrest the sweep of the winds through it. In the 1920s Masonic Street was extended across the Panhandle by voter-approved ordinance, over the objections of the Park Commission. The William McKinley Monument by Robert Ingersoll Aitken, bronze and marble on granite, 1904, the gift of the McKinley Monument Committee, stands at Fell Street and Baker Street; the fifteen-foot bronze figure at the top of the pedestal represents Justice. McKinley was shot on 6 September 1901 and died on 14 September 1901.

places.name: The Music Concourse
places.summary: The sunken oval at the east end of the park, with the de Young Museum on its north side and the California Academy of Sciences on its south. The bowl sits approximately ten feet below the surrounding roadway; its surface is asphalt paths with fields of decomposed granite at its southwest end and turf at its northeast end, planted with a bosque of pollarded deciduous trees, primarily London Plane and Scotch Elm. Three pedestrian tunnels run under the concourse, and the ordinance designating San Francisco Landmark No. 249 draws the landmark boundary to include them.
places.history: The concourse was laid out following the 1894 Mid Winter Fair and dates as a site to 1900. Monuments stand around it: the Miguel de Cervantes Memorial by Joseph Jacinto Mora, bronze and natural stone, 1916, showing Cervantes looking down at Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, who kneel before him; two cast concrete sphinxes by Arthur Putnam of 1903 flanking the footpath entrance to the de Young parking area; the Robert Emmet Memorial by Jerome Connor, bronze on granite, 1919, the gift of James D. Phelan, at whose dedication Eamon De Valera, President of the Irish Republic in 1919, spoke; the Ludwig van Beethoven Monument of 1915, the gift of the Beethoven Maennerchor of New York, dedicated on 15 August 1915; the Goethe and Schiller Monument by Ernst Rietschel, 1901; the Giuseppe Verdi Monument by Orazio Grossoni, a 52-ton statue given by the Italian Colony of San Francisco; the Rideout Fountain by M. Earl Cummings, a saber-toothed tiger in combat with a cobra-headed serpent, the bequest of Corinne Rideout; the Pool of Enchantment by M. Earl Cummings, a young Indian boy playing a musical pipe to two listening California mountain lions, east of the de Young Museum; the U. S. Grant Memorial by Rupert Schmid; the Sundial by M. Earl Cummings, the gift of the National Society of Colonial Dames of America in California; the Roman Gladiator by Guillaumo Geefs; the Lion by R. Hinton Perry; and the Cider Press by Thomas Shields-Clarke, purchased by M. H. de Young. The Page Fountains of 1914, two circular reflecting pools with granite coping, were a gift of the widow of Charles Page, and the Phoebe Hearst Fountain of 1926 is a cast stone double tier fountain with a pair of flanking classical staircases. The North Tunnel under John F. Kennedy Drive, designed by Coxhead & Coxhead in 1897, is approximately 130 feet long, with carved Rocklin granite arches loosely based on the Arch of Titus.

places.name: Spreckels Temple of Music
places.summary: The bandshell at the west end of the Music Concourse, a masonry and concrete structure clad on the exterior with Colusa sandstone, consisting of a central half-dome bandshell with two flanking colonnades of eight pairs of Ionic columns. Its spandrels are recorded in the city's Civic Art Collection as the work of Robert Ingersoll Aitken, in cast concrete.
places.history: Built in 1900 with funds donated by the sugar magnate Claus Spreckels and designed by the Reid Brothers, architects. It was damaged in 1906 and again in 1989, and an extensive restoration and seismic upgrade was completed in 1994.

places.name: de Young Museum
places.address: 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, San Francisco, CA 94118
places.summary: The art museum on the north side of the Music Concourse, at 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. Keith Haring's Untitled (Three Dancing Figures), enamel on aluminum, stands at the museum; the city's Civic Art Collection dates it 2001 (fabricated in 1989).
places.history: The museum began as the Fine Arts building of the 1894 Mid Winter Fair, an Egyptian Revival structure given to the Park Commission. It was rebuilt in a Spanish Plateresque manner in 1919; the central section and the tower were added in 1921 and the west wing in 1925. The 1894 building was deemed unsafe and demolished in 1929. The Brundidge wing and a rear expansion were added in 1965, and those buildings were demolished in 2003. La poeme de la vigne, a bronze by Paul Gustave Dore created in 1877 and 1878, was a gift of M. H. de Young.

places.name: California Academy of Sciences
places.address: 55 Music Concourse Drive, San Francisco, CA 94118
places.summary: The natural history museum on the south side of the Music Concourse, at 55 Music Concourse Drive. It is open Monday to Saturday from 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and holds Thursday NightLife from 6 to 10 p.m. for visitors of 21 and over. Its named venues are the Steinhart Aquarium, the Morrison Planetarium, the Osher Rainforest, a four-story rainforest housed in a glass dome, the Kimball Natural History Museum and a living roof. The Steinhart holds a 212,000-gallon living coral reef and over 1,000 animal species.
places.history: The Academy's buildings on this site went up in sequence: the North American Hall, now Wild California, followed by the Steinhart Aquarium in 1923, Simson African Hall in 1934, the Morrison Planetarium in 1952, Cowell Hall in 1969, Wattis Hall in 1976, the Fish Roundabout in 1977 and Life Through Time in 1990. Two bronze portrait reliefs by Edgar Walters were commissioned by the architect Lewis Hobart upon construction of the Steinhart Aquarium in 1923. Maya Lin's Where the Land Meets the Sea, marine grade stainless steel of 2008, was commissioned for the Academy.

places.name: Japanese Tea Garden
places.address: 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, San Francisco, CA 94118
places.summary: The tea garden at 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, open every day: 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. in winter, when the gate closes at 4:30 p.m., and 9 a.m. to 5:45 p.m. in summer, when the gate closes at 5:30 p.m. It holds a five-story pagoda, a tea house, a dry landscape garden and the bronze Buddha Amazarasti-no-Hotoke.
places.history: The garden was created by George Turner Marsh as a Japanese Village feature of the 1894 Mid Winter Exposition and was designed and constructed by Makoto Hagiwara. Originally one acre in size, it was expanded to five acres in 1902, and Hagiwara designed the expanded garden; the Hagiwara family continued to live and work in the garden until 1942, when the family was interned during the Second World War. The Main Gate is dated 1894 and was reconstructed in 1985, as was the South Gate. The five-story pagoda was originally constructed for a Japanese village at the 1915 Panama Pacific International Exposition, the tea house was built for the Mid-Winter Exposition of 1894, and the dry landscape garden was designed in 1953 by Nagao Sakurai. Amazarasti-no-Hotoke, the bronze Buddha, was cast in 1790 in Tajima Province on Honshu for the Taioriji Temple and placed in the garden in 1945, the gift of the S. & G. Gump Company in memory of A. Livingston Gump. A plaque to the Hagiwara family by Ruth Asawa, bronze on rock, 1974, was a gift of the John McLaren Society for the Japanese Tea Garden.

places.name: Conservatory of Flowers
places.summary: The wood and glass conservatory above Conservatory Valley, north of John F. Kennedy Drive. Its galleries are the Aquatic Plants, Highland Tropics, Lowland Tropics, Potted Plants and West galleries. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 50, designated in 1972, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, reference number 71000184.
places.history: The conservatory was acquired for the park from an estate while it was still in crates and was constructed in 1878. A fire damaged the building in 1883, with repairs that enlarged it made by 1885, and the wood and glass building was damaged by storms in 1995.

places.name: Conservatory Valley
places.summary: The sunken lawn below the Conservatory of Flowers, with the Dahlia Garden of 1939 in the centre of the conservatory access drive turnaround, planted with numerous varieties of dahlias, San Francisco's official flower. The Arizona Garden of 1894, a historic collection of succulent plants, lies east of the conservatory.
places.history: The valley was graded in 1872 under the direction of William Hammond Hall as a setting for a conservatory, and was sunk to provide additional shelter from the strong ocean winds. It was paved between 1882 and sometime in the 1890s. A concrete tunnel of about 1890, with a retaining wall and balustrade, runs under the main drive on axis with the conservatory. The James A. Garfield Monument, bronze on granite by Frank Happersberger, 1885, acquired by public subscription, stands on a knoll east of the conservatory on John F. Kennedy Drive.

places.name: Tree Fern Dell
places.summary: A planting of Australian tree ferns across John F. Kennedy Drive from Conservatory Valley, made in 1939.
places.history: The National Register nomination records that Australian tree ferns were reportedly brought to the park by Alice Eastwood, Curator of Botany at the California Academy of Sciences.

places.name: Koret Children's Quarter
places.summary: The children's playground below the Sharon Building, with a carousel in its own building. Five cast concrete animal sculptures by Vicki Saulls of 2007, a yellow crab, a pink crab, a purple crab, a pelican and a tortoise, were commissioned by the San Francisco Arts Commission and are carried in the city's Civic Art Collection as Untitled (group of animals).
places.history: The playground dates from about 1888. The Foresters of America Memorial, a marble fountain of 1927 just west of the Sharon Building, honours foresters killed in the First World War, 1917 to 1919. The Sarah B. Cooper Memorial, sandstone on concrete by Jack Moxom, 1939, stands at the picnic area in the meadow beside the playground.

places.name: Sharon Building
places.summary: The sandstone building above the Children's Quarter, in a Richardsonian Romanesque manner, now in use as an art centre. San Francisco Landmark No. 124, designated in 1981.
places.history: Built in 1888 to designs by the architects George W. Percy and Frederick F. Hamilton. It was severely damaged in the 1906 earthquake and was rebuilt according to the original plans; a fire damaged the building in 1974, and a phased restoration was completed in 1992.

places.name: Golden Gate Park Carousel
places.summary: The carousel in the Children's Quarter, housed in a building of 1889 designed by the architect Arthur Page Brown: essentially a circular Greek temple with its domed roof supported by sixteen fluted, tapered wood Doric columns. Open-air at first, it was given a glass and metal enclosure in 1964, and a rehabilitation in 2002 gave it a new metal roof. A ticket pavilion of 1889 stands with it.
places.history: The carousel was built in 1914 by the Herschell-Spillman Company of North Tonawanda, New York. It operated in Lincoln Park in Los Angeles and was used at the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition before being purchased and installed in Golden Gate Park in 1941. It was restored in 1984.

places.name: Alvord Lake
places.summary: A small lake by the Haight Street entrance, lined with concrete and rocks and holding a small island.
places.history: Park Commissioner William Alvord donated $200 for construction of a lily pond to grow hardy lilies; the pond was made in 1882 and enlarged in 1889. Unlike other park lakes, which are lined with clay, it is lined with concrete.

places.name: Alvord Lake Bridge
places.summary: The bridge by the Haight Street entrance, an ornamental structure with an imitation stone finish on its exterior and concrete stalactites hanging from inside its 20-foot span. The National Register nomination records that Alvord Bridge was designated a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark in 1969.
places.history: The bridge was built in 1889 to a design by the engineer Ernest Ransome, in the same year that the lily pond William Alvord had funded in 1882 was enlarged.

places.name: Robin Williams Meadow
places.summary: Robin Williams Meadow, which the nomination records as Sharon Meadow, is a bowl-shaped meadow of about 1880 below the Sharon Building.
places.history: The Sarah B. Cooper Memorial, sandstone on concrete by Jack Moxom, 1939, stands at the meadow's picnic area near the Children's Quarter.

places.name: Kezar Stadium
places.summary: Kezar Stadium stands at 670 Kezar Drive. The gates are by Alan Fleming, galvanized metal, each 138 inches high.
places.history: The first stadium on the site was built in 1924 on the ground of the former park nursery and was expanded in 1928 to a seating capacity of 65,000. It was home of the San Francisco Forty-niners until 1969. The concrete stands were demolished in 1989 and the stadium was rebuilt in 1990.

places.name: Kezar Pavilion
places.summary: Kezar Pavilion is a gymnasium building of 1926 with seats for four thousand, in the Spanish Mission style, of cast concrete walls with steel framing and a tile roof. Willis Polk was also involved in the design. The building fronts on Stanyan Street.
places.history: The pavilion and Kezar Stadium stand together on the ground between Stanyan Street and Kezar Drive, which the park nursery occupied until 1924.

places.name: McLaren Lodge
places.summary: The lodge at the Stanyan Street end of the park, in a Moorish-Gothic style, its exterior walls 18 inches thick in ashlar basalt masonry with sandstone quoins. It is the administrative headquarters of the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department. San Francisco Landmark No. 175, designated in 1984.
places.history: Built in 1896 to house the then Park Commission and as a residence for Superintendent John McLaren, who lived in the Lodge for forty-seven years, and designed in a Moorish-Gothic style by the architect Edward R. Swain. A yellow brick and glass annex was added in 1950 and is connected to the Lodge by a breezeway.

places.name: Arguello Gate
places.summary: The park gate at Fulton Street and Arguello Boulevard: two large pylons and flanking walls of stone ornamented with polychrome terra cotta and copper metal urns and globes.
places.history: The gate was built in 1915 and was a gift of Philomen Clark in memory of Crawford W. Clark.

places.name: Brown Gate
places.summary: The park entrance at 8th Avenue and Fulton Street, with a bronze Bear on the northeast corner and a bronze Lion on the northwest corner.
places.history: Bear and Lion are both by M. Earl Cummings, bronze on sandstone, 1908, the gift of Suzanna Brown, at 8th Avenue and Fulton Street. In 1948 the road needed widening, so the gateway was moved several feet apart.

places.name: The Stanyan and Fulton Street wall
places.summary: A stone masonry wall of rustic stone-like rectangular blocks with a concrete cap, extending along Stanyan Street from Fell Street and along Fulton Street to 2nd Avenue.
places.history: The wall dates from about 1902.

places.name: Golden Gate Park tennis courts
places.summary: The tennis courts at the east end of the park, by the Children's Quarter.
places.history: Eight tennis courts were installed in 1901. As of 1935 there were twenty-one.

places.name: Lawn Bowling Clubhouse and Greens
places.summary: The lawn bowling clubhouse and its greens at the east end of the park; the clubhouse is a flat-roofed, wood frame Edwardian style building. San Francisco Landmark No. 181, designated in 1986.
places.history: The first green was constructed in 1901, a second green for women was built in 1913, and a third was completed in 1928. The clubhouse was built in 1915 to replace an earlier clubhouse dating to 1902, and an extension was added in 1971.

places.name: Big Rec
places.summary: The baseball grounds at the east end of the park, approximately 12 acres, with two regulation diamonds with skinned infields and concrete stands. The grandstands are named in honour of James Nealon, founder of a benefit fund for injured ballplayers, and Charles Graham of the San Francisco Seals.
places.history: The grounds appear on William Hammond Hall's 1870 plan and were officially developed in 1893. The large open meadow once held as many as nine baseball games. The east stands were constructed in 1950. A concrete handball building with a glass skylight roof, of 1902 to 1937, stands nearby, along with sixteen horseshoe courts reportedly first developed on that site in 1922 and a monumental bas relief concrete horse created in 1937 by Jesse Anderson of the Horseshoe Club.

places.name: Shakespeare Garden
places.summary: A garden of approximately half an acre whose focal point is a brick wall containing six bronze panels with 88 floral quotations from Shakespeare's plays and a recessed case holding a bronze bust of Shakespeare. A cast iron and limestone sundial by L. Cardini stands at its centre.
places.history: The garden was created in 1928 from an idea of Alice Eastwood, Curator of Botany at the California Academy of Sciences. The bust was a gift from the citizens of Stratford-on-Avon, England, and is a copy of the cast made in 1814 by George Bullock. The sundial was installed in 1928.

places.name: National AIDS Memorial Grove
places.summary: The memorial grove in the de Laveaga Dell, with a rockery cascade fed by a natural seasonal spring under a canopy of oaks.
places.history: The dell was developed into a landscape feature in 1902 by John McLaren, with funds donated by Joseph de Laveaga; McLaren used a natural seasonal spring and created a rockery cascade under the canopy of oaks. Before that the site was called the Deer Glen and was a fenced compound housing the park's deer collection. The area fell into disuse and became overgrown until 1991, when a volunteer group chose the site for the AIDS Memorial Grove.

places.name: Powell Street Railway Shelter
places.summary: A gable-roofed rectangular shelter open at both ends, its walls a combination of wood, concrete and brick, its roof structure of exposed heavy timber trusses with mortise and tenon joints. It now serves as a pedestrian entrance to the park.
places.history: It was constructed in 1889 as a gateway to the park for riders of the Powell Street Cable Car and served the railroad until 1906.

places.name: John McLaren Memorial Rhododendron Dell
places.summary: A rhododendron planting stretching across 25 acres on the north-facing slope of the park's middle ridge.
places.history: It was started in 1942 and named the John McLaren Memorial Rhododendron Dell after McLaren's death in 1943. The bronze statue of John McLaren by M. Earl Cummings stands at ground level, without the standard granite pedestal: the superintendent refused to accept the statue made in his honour, and the work stood on the sculptor's doorstep for years until its placement in 1944 after McLaren's death.

places.name: Pioneer Log Cabin
places.summary: A cabin constructed of unpeeled redwood logs from Humboldt County, with two rustic masonry chimneys, near the Stow Lake entrance off John F. Kennedy Drive.
places.history: It was built in 1911 as a meeting house for the Association of Pioneer Women of California, expanded in 1931 and restored in 1995. The Pioneer Mother, a bronze by Charles Grafly created in 1914 and exhibited at the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition, was installed nearby in 1940.

places.name: Prayer Book Cross
places.summary: A sandstone cross 57 feet high, modelled after a Celtic cross on the Scottish island of Iona, standing on a hill north of John F. Kennedy Drive opposite 20th Avenue.
places.history: Designed by Ernest Coxhead and erected by the Northern California Episcopal Diocese to commemorate the religious service in the English language held by Francis Fletcher, chaplain to Sir Francis Drake, on the shores of Drake's Bay on 24 June 1579. It was unveiled on the opening day of the Mid Winter Fair, 1 January 1894.

places.name: Heroes Redwood Grove
places.summary: A 15-acre memorial grove on the north side of the park between 10th Avenue and Park Presidio Boulevard, holding the Gold Star Mothers Rock, a 20-ton boulder brought from Twin Peaks.
places.history: The grove was planted in 1939 and the boulder was placed in 1932.

places.name: Redwood Memorial Grove and Doughboy Meadow
places.summary: A grove of 37 redwood trees, one for each fallen member, north of John F. Kennedy Drive near 16th Avenue, with the Doughboy standing in the meadow: a bronze by M. Earl Cummings of a hatless male figure holding a wreath to his chest, flanked by two wood flag poles.
places.history: The grove was planted in 1930.

places.name: Rose Garden
places.summary: A rose garden of double rows of rectangular beds on John F. Kennedy Drive, with the bust of Thomas Masaryk by J. Matatka, bronze and granite of 1962, at its entrance.
places.history: The garden was developed in 1961 on the site of what was once a roadway between 14th Avenue and John F. Kennedy Drive; the roadway was removed when the Park Presidio Bypass was built in 1939. The Masaryk bust had previously been exhibited at the 1939 World's Fair on Treasure Island.

places.name: San Francisco Botanical Garden
places.summary: The botanical garden at 1199 9th Avenue: 55 developed acres of a 70-acre site, showing more than 8,000 different kinds of plants. Its collections include the Andean Cloud Forest, Australia, California, Chile, Mediterranean, Mesoamerican Cloud Forest, New Zealand, South Africa, Southeast Asia Cloud Forest and Temperate Asia gardens, with camellias, high elevation palms, magnolias and rhododendrons, and the Ancient Plants, Moon Viewing Garden, Children's Garden, Conifer Lawn, Celebration Garden, Fountain Plaza, Garden of Fragrance, Great Meadow, Succulent Garden and Zellerbach Garden. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: John McLaren proposed an arboretum on this site in 1890, based on the idea of Harvard University's Arnold Arboretum. In 1926 Helene Strybing gave a gift to the Park Commission for development of the arboretum as a memorial to her late husband Christian Strybing; a 1930s master plan established the design concepts, and the arboretum opened in May 1940. St. Francis of Assisi (Feeding the Birds), a bronze by Clara Huntington created in 1939, was the gift of the artist in 1958, and a granite stupa carried in the city's Civic Art Collection as Unknown (Granite stupa) stands in the garden.

places.name: San Francisco County Fair Building
places.summary: A Mid-century Modern building at the Botanical Garden, of cast concrete walls scored into blocks with a metal pan roof, containing an auditorium, meeting rooms, exhibition space and offices. The Helen Crocker Russell Library of Horticulture is an extension of it.
places.history: Built in 1960 as the Hall of Flowers to designs by the architects Appleton and Wolfard; the name was changed in 1986 to avoid confusion with the Conservatory of Flowers. The library was designed by the firm of Yuill-Thorton, Warner and Levikow and was dedicated in 1972.

places.name: Stow Lake
places.summary: A lake of 12.7 acres encircling Strawberry Hill, crossed by two bridges of 1893 by the architect Arthur Page Brown: the Roman Bridge, a gentle arch of iron-reinforced, smooth-finished concrete on the north side, and the Rustic Stone Bridge, a more steeply arching pedestrian bridge covered with bulging rustic stones, over the south arm.
places.history: Stow Lake was completed, along with Huntington Falls, in 1893, and was built as an overflow lake for a reservoir set on top of Strawberry Hill. It was constructed with a 10-inch layer of clay, on top of which was placed a 3-inch layer of crushed rock that was rolled into the clay.

places.name: Strawberry Hill
places.summary: The island hill inside Stow Lake, with Huntington Falls on its flank and the Chinese Pavilion at its foot.
places.history: Before the construction of Stow Lake, Strawberry Hill was known as The Island because it was a vegetated hill in a sea of sand, and a carriage road traversed up its side. The ruin of the Sweeney Observatory stands on it: a two-story circular stone structure for viewing, built in 1891 with funds donated by Thomas U. Sweeney, destroyed in the 1906 earthquake and never rebuilt, of which the circular concrete foundation and a few of the building stones remain.

places.name: Stow Lake Boathouse
places.summary: The boathouse at the north part of Stow Lake, a gabled building with horizontal wood siding and an asphalt-shingled roof. It rents American-made row and pedal boats by the hour and runs a cafe serving from lattes to local wine and from hamburgers to salads. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The boathouse was first constructed in 1893 and rebuilt in 1946. It provides space for boat rentals, a food concession, a gardeners' office and a concession office.

places.name: Huntington Falls
places.summary: A cascade approximately 90 feet high on the flank of Strawberry Hill, of concrete sculpted to look like natural rock.
places.history: The falls were completed with Stow Lake in 1893 and are named in honour of the railroad magnate Collis P. Huntington. In 1962 a broken irrigation line undermined much of the concrete foundations, causing a collapse, and the falls were completely reconstructed in 1984.

places.name: Chinese Pavilion
places.summary: A wood and concrete Chinese-style moon-viewing platform at Stow Lake.
places.history: It was built in 1981, a gift from San Francisco's sister city Taipei, Taiwan.

places.name: The Polo Field
places.summary: The oval in the middle of the park, formally the Golden Gate Park Stadium. A 10-foot-high graded berm, with a trotting track on top, encloses the 17-acre field; eighteen sections of concrete stands line the embankment on the north side and another six sections on the south side.
places.history: The stadium was built between 1906 and 1909 to a design by the architect brothers James and Merritt Reid. One 200-foot-long experimental section of the grand stadium was built in 1909. It included a trotting track on the outside perimeter, a cinder path for bicycles inside the stadium, and space for polo and football in the centre, large enough for six football fields.

places.name: Golden Gate Park Stables
places.summary: A quadrangle of stables around a central riding ring, the buildings concrete with gabled clay tile roofs. The grandstand structure was built in 1909 as part of the Golden Gate Park Stadium.
places.history: The stables were a Works Progress Administration project completed in 1939. The Park Police Stables of 1936 stand nearby: a two-story concrete T-shaped building with a red tile roof and a copper cupola on the ridgeline, housing the San Francisco Police Department's mounted unit horses, renovated in 1995.

places.name: Anglers' Lodge and Fly Casting Pools
places.summary: A single-story wood frame rustic building on a rise overlooking the fly casting pools, its shutters carved with a fish motif. The pools are concrete with sloping sides, 450 feet wide by 185 feet long, and are divided into three sections.
places.history: The lodge was constructed in 1936 with Works Progress Administration funds and is home to the Golden Gate Anglers and Casting Club, which was founded in 1890.

places.name: Lloyd Lake
places.summary: A naturalistic reflecting pond 1.4 acres in size, with the Portals of the Past standing at its edge: the stone portico of the former mansion of A. N. Towne, President of the Southern Pacific Railroad.
places.history: The lake was made in 1892 and is named in honour of Ruben Lloyd, 1835 to 1909, park commissioner. The Towne mansion, designed by the architect Arthur Page Brown, stood at California and Taylor streets until it was destroyed by the fire resulting from the 1906 earthquake; the portico was donated to the park and erected in 1909.

places.name: Speedway Meadow
places.summary: A long meadow in the western half of the park, on the line of the old speed road. Little Speedway Meadow, the western remnant of the same road, lies between Chain of Lakes Drive and the Polo Field.
places.history: A speed road was completed in 1894 as a place to race horses; it was a straight road nine-tenths of a mile long. The site was used as a camp for a while after the 1906 earthquake, after which it was returned to park use as a meadow. The rest of the road was removed with the construction of the Polo Field in 1906.

places.name: Spreckels Lake
places.summary: A lake approximately six acres in size, used for model boating. Unlike other lakes in the park, it is surrounded by a concrete edge and sidewalk.
places.history: The lake was made in 1904.

places.name: San Francisco Model Yacht Club
places.summary: The model yacht clubhouse on Spreckels Lake, of concrete walls with a hipped red tile roof, with two attached restrooms flanking the building. The club gives its own location as the 36th Avenue and Fulton Street entrance to the park.
places.history: The clubhouse was constructed in 1938 to house the boats of the San Francisco Model Yacht Club, replacing an earlier clubhouse built in 1904.

places.name: Golden Gate Park Senior Center
places.summary: A building of scored concrete with cast stone quoins at the corners and a glazed tile roof, with a semicircular driveway connecting it to Fulton Street.
places.history: It was built in 1932 as the San Francisco Police Training Academy and was converted to a senior center in 1965.

places.name: Bison Paddock
places.summary: A large fenced open space in the western half of the park holding the park's bison, with a feeding shelter and isolation pens at its west end. A 1.2-acre dog training field, surrounded by a low chain link fence, lies behind the paddock.
places.history: Buffalo, correctly called bison, were introduced into the park in 1890 as part of a national effort to prevent their extinction, and were initially placed in a paddock near the de Laveaga Dell. The small herd was moved to the present ground around 1900. The dog training field dates from 1905.

places.name: Chain of Lakes
places.summary: Three lakes in the western half of the park: North Lake of 3.8 acres, Middle Lake of 1.3 acres and South Lake of 1.1 acres. North Lake holds several small islands planted with wetland trees such as swamp cypress, weeping willows and alders; Middle Lake is well hidden by tules and other dense planting.
places.history: The three lakes were made in 1898. The rustic bridges that once connected North Lake's islands are no longer present, and an extensive rehabilitation of that lake was completed in 2004.

places.name: Breon Gate
places.summary: The park gate at 19th Avenue and Lincoln Way: two large ornamented stone pylons. The inscription records that the gateway was dedicated by Cristine Breon to all who enter the park, 1924.
places.history: The gate was built in 1924.

places.name: Dutch Windmill
places.summary: The windmill at the northwest corner of the park, near the Great Highway. The structure is 75 feet tall and has a 5-foot-thick concrete foundation with a diameter of 33 feet; the tower is a wood frame structure covered with wood shingles. San Francisco Landmark No. 147, designated in 1981, and recorded on the Article 10 register as Dutch Windmill (North Windmill).
places.history: It was built in 1902 to pump water from wells near the windmill to the reservoir on Strawberry Hill, after the Park Commission approved development of a windmill of the Holland type. It was designed by Alpheus Bull, Jr., a mechanical engineer from the Union Iron Works, and had a capacity of 30,000 gallons per hour. The pumps were electrified in 1913, and during the Second World War the internal machinery was removed for the scrap metal drive. Funds were donated for a rehabilitation, which was completed in 1981 after several years of work donated by the U.S. Navy Construction Battalion. A caretaker's cottage was built next to the mill in 1903 and was demolished sometime after 1935.

places.name: Queen Wilhelmina Tulip Garden
places.summary: A tulip garden beside the Dutch Windmill at the west end of the park.
places.history: The garden was named in honour of Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands upon her death in 1962.

places.name: Murphy Windmill
places.summary: The windmill at the southwest corner of the park, 95 feet tall with a span of 114 feet. It has a massive concrete foundation supporting a wood-framed tower covered with slate roofing shingles, and is sometimes referred to as the English Windmill. San Francisco Landmark No. 210, designated in 2000, recorded on the Article 10 register as Murphy Windmill and Millwright's Cottage.
places.history: It was built in 1905 with funds donated by Samuel Murphy, with a capacity of 40,000 gallons per hour, and was said to be designed after English style windmills. The windmill was not used for pumping water after 1913, when electric pumps were installed.

places.name: Millwright's House
places.summary: A small two-story brick building with a slate shingle roof beside the Murphy Windmill, designed by the Reid Brothers. It is part of San Francisco Landmark No. 210, designated in 2000 and recorded on the Article 10 register as Murphy Windmill and Millwright's Cottage.
places.history: The building was built in 1909.

places.name: Beach Chalet
places.summary: A stucco Spanish-Moorish revival pavilion at 1000 Great Highway, at the west end of the park, with a visitor center on the ground floor and a restaurant above. Its interior carries the fresco People and Places of San Francisco by Lucien Labaudt, 1936, made for the Works Progress Administration's Federal Art Project, along with mosaics and wood carvings. San Francisco Landmark No. 179, designated in 1985; listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 22 July 1981, reference number 81000172.
places.history: The building of 1925 is the second structure of that name on the Great Highway; the first Beach Chalet was built in 1900 on the west side of the Great Highway and was removed in 1925. It was designed by Willis Polk. The upper floor housed a restaurant and the lower floor a public lounge and changing rooms for visitors to the beach. The interior was significantly enhanced in 1936 and 1937 with the addition of frescoes, mosaics and wood carvings designed by the San Francisco artist Lucien Labaudt. The building was used by the Army during the Second World War. The city closed it for renovations in 1981; the artwork underwent a restoration in 1987, and the building remained closed to the public until December 1996, when it reopened with a restaurant on the second floor and a visitor center on the ground floor.

places.name: Beach Chalet Brewery & Restaurant
places.summary: The brewery and restaurant on the upper floor of the Beach Chalet, at 1000 Great Highway. It is open Monday to Friday from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. and Saturday and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m., with happy hour on weekdays from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. and weekend brunch from 10 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.
places.history: The upper floor of the building housed a restaurant when it was completed in 1925. The city closed the building for renovations in 1981, and it reopened in December 1996 with a restaurant on the second floor.

places.name: Roald Amundsen Monument
places.summary: A monument of red Norwegian granite and bronze by Hans Jauchen, north of the Beach Chalet, with a second bronze plaque of 2000 by John and Rolph Kricken.
places.history: The monument honours Roald Amundsen, who completed the crossing of the Northwest Passage in 1906, making the voyage around the top of North America in a small sloop, the Gjoa, and completing the journey in San Francisco. The crew was honoured by the city and the Gjoa was placed at Ocean Beach. The monument was dedicated in 1929, and the Gjoa remained at the monument until 1972, when it was returned to Norway.

places.name: Golden Gate Park Golf Course
places.summary: A nine-hole golf course of about 20 acres in the western half of the park, with a clubhouse of the 1950s: a small, flat-roofed, one-story building whose flat roof cantilevers to cover the adjacent walkway.
places.history: The course was created in 1951.

places.name: Archery Field
places.summary: A meadow approximately four acres in size near the 47th Avenue entrance from Fulton Street, with archery targets at its east end.
places.history: The field dates from 1938.

places.name: Beach Chalet Soccer Fields
places.summary: Soccer fields southeast of the Beach Chalet, at the west end of the park.
places.history: Soccer fields have stood on this site since at least 1935.

places.name: Western park entry monuments
places.summary: Two large boulder groupings inscribed with the name Golden Gate Park, one at the Great Highway and John F. Kennedy Drive entry and one at the Fulton Street and Martin Luther King Jr. Drive entry.
places.history: The two groupings date from about 1998.

places.name: Ninth Avenue playground
places.summary: A playground at Fulton Street and Ninth Avenue, at the north end of the tunnel under John F. Kennedy Drive.
places.history: No source states the year the playground was built, so none is given here.

places.name: 46th Avenue playground
places.summary: A playground at 46th Avenue and Lincoln Way, at the south side of the park.
places.history: No source states the year the playground was built, so none is given here.

entries.name: California Academy of Sciences
entries.note: Open 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday to Saturday and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Sunday at 55 Music Concourse Drive, with Thursday NightLife from 6 to 10 p.m.

entries.name: de Young Museum
entries.note: The art museum at 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, on the north side of the Music Concourse; no source states its opening hours.

entries.name: Japanese Tea Garden
entries.note: At 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, with a five-story pagoda, a tea house of 1894, a dry landscape garden of 1953 and a bronze Buddha cast in 1790.

entries.name: Conservatory of Flowers
entries.note: The wood and glass conservatory of 1878: San Francisco Landmark No. 50, designated in 1972, and listed on the National Register in 1971, reference number 71000184.

entries.name: San Francisco Botanical Garden
entries.note: At 1199 9th Avenue: 55 developed acres of a 70-acre site, showing more than 8,000 different kinds of plants, opened in May 1940.

entries.name: The Music Concourse
entries.note: The sunken oval between the two museums, planted with London Plane and Scotch Elm: San Francisco Landmark No. 249, designated in 2005.

entries.name: Stow Lake
entries.note: A lake of 12.7 acres around Strawberry Hill, crossed by the Roman Bridge and the Rustic Stone Bridge, both of 1893 by Arthur Page Brown.

entries.name: The Panhandle
entries.note: A strip one block wide and eight blocks long between Oak Street and Fell Street, with a bicycle path on the north side and a footpath on the south.

entries.name: Dutch Windmill
entries.note: Built in 1902 to pump water to the Strawberry Hill reservoir, 75 feet tall: San Francisco Landmark No. 147, designated in 1981.

entries.name: Murphy Windmill
entries.note: Built in 1905, 95 feet tall with a span of 114 feet: San Francisco Landmark No. 210, designated in 2000, with the Millwright's Cottage.

entries.name: Beach Chalet Brewery & Restaurant
entries.note: On the upper floor at 1000 Great Highway, open 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekdays and 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. at weekends, with brunch from 10 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.

entries.name: Stow Lake Boathouse
entries.note: Row and pedal boats by the hour at the north part of Stow Lake, with a cafe serving from lattes to local wine and from hamburgers to salads.

entries.name: Koret Children's Quarter
entries.note: The playground of about 1888 below the Sharon Building, with five cast concrete animals by Vicki Saulls of 2007 and the carousel beside it.

entries.name: Bison Paddock
entries.note: The fenced paddock in the western half of the park; bison came to the park in 1890 and the herd was moved to this ground around 1900.
